summary: Lake Huron light at the eastern approach to the Straits of Mackinac: a stone tower fell in 1837, the brick tower of 1867 still stands, and it has been private since 1925.

structures.type: square tower attached to the lakeward end of the dwelling
structures.note: Third Bois Blanc tower; yellow-brick dwelling and square tower (LighthouseFriends).
Stone tower of about sixty-five feet with a detached dwelling; undermined and fell in a storm in December 1837.
Second tower, built farther from the lake; fourth-order Fresnel from 1857 (LighthouseFriends).
Black skeletal tower near the shore (about 46 ft) after 1924; moved to a white skeletal tower in 1942; cylindrical tower erected near the lighthouse in 1986.

access.note: Privately owned; grounds, dwelling and tower closed. Best viewed from the water (LighthouseFriends).

visit.note: Seasonal ferry service runs to the island; eastbound lighthouse cruises pass the light (LighthouseFriends).

events.note: Congress appropriated $5,000 for a lighthouse on the island, 23 May 1828.
Stone tower and detached dwelling completed in 1829 (LighthouseFriends); USLHS gives 1829 as the year established.
Placed into service in the spring of 1830 (LighthouseFriends). The station record and USLHS give 1829.
Stone tower undermined by high water and fell in a storm in December 1837.
Second, thirty-five-foot stone tower; Congress allocated $5,000 for rebuilding on 7 July 1838.
Fourth-order Fresnel lens in the stone tower (LighthouseFriends). USLHS gives 1867 for the original lens.
Yellow-brick dwelling with a square tower; Congress granted $14,000 on 2 March 1867.
USLHS record gives 1867 for the original lens.
Boathouse moved to a sheltered location on the south side of the island.
Brick cistern built in the cellar (Board report 1891-1892).
Life-Saving Service stations at Marquette and Bois Blanc Island completed and put in operation (fiscal 1891 report). The Bois Blanc surfmen's station is a separate station record.
Steamer warned off by the surfmen's night signal; the report's warnings table is headed 1891.
Coast Guard crew took all aboard the Colonial off after she was caught in ice floes on 20 April 1922.
Light changed to flashing (Lighthouse Service Bulletin index 1924-1929; the index gives no year, the station was discontinued in 1924).
Sold to a private owner on 24 August 1925.
Light moved to a white skeletal tower, a better daymark.
Cylindrical tower erected near the lighthouse.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: USLHS gives 1829 as the year established; LighthouseFriends says the stone tower and dwelling were completed in 1829 and the light went into service in the spring of 1830. The story gives both.
LighthouseFriends says a fourth-order Fresnel was installed in the stone tower in 1857. USLHS gives 1867 for the original lens. Unresolved; the story reports both.

notes_for_editor: Keeper identity: the USLHS roster gives 'Eber Brock Ward (1829-1843)' as keeper, but LighthouseFriends calls the keeper Eber Ward and names Eber Brock (E.B.) Ward as his son, the Detroit shipping millionaire. Not settled; the story calls the keeper 'Eber Ward' per LighthouseFriends and names the roster entry in the keepers list only. Check before publication. Emily Ward's account is recorded in Hurlbut's 1889 book, years after the storm, so it is a remembered account, and the story says so. Her brother's name is only 'Bolivar' in the text, so no relationship is stated. County: the station record says Mackinac County; the USLHS record says Cheboygan. Not changed. The Life-Saving Service 'Bois Blanc' station is a separate station on the island; its wrecks are not all tied to the light. A wreck entry in the 1892 report ('Bois Blanc, Lake Huron. Sunk. The crew of five escaped in their boat') has no date or vessel name in the text read, so it is not used. The date of the steamer warning is taken by column position from an OCR'd table ('Aug. 24' against Bois Blanc), so the story gives only the year the table is headed. The Board's 'dangerous reef' sentence is from OCR ('many vessels have met disa^ ter'), so the quote is limited to 'This dangerous reef runs out'. The 1922 Colonial rescue and the 1924 change to flashing rest on LighthouseFriends or the bulletin index only; the Chronicling America search for Metivier and the Colonial returned no pages. The Cheboygan 'Northern Tribune' pages returned for 1875-1882 do not describe the light, so no newspaper is cited. Shape: six chapters, each with sourced material, at about moderate length (the guide's moderate shape is 2-4 chapters). The editor may collapse the shape to fewer chapters. Fact-check 2026-10-27: the Hurlbut book's title page reads 'Cambridge, 1889' with no 'privately printed' line, so the footnote no longer claims it. The story says the Emily Ward account is printed in the book as her own speech, and it is dated to 1889, not the storm. The first-light sentence no longer says the sources disagree on 1829 or 1830; the 1829 and 1830 dates are set out in the Building chapter. The 1892 steamer line is the Life-Saving Service station's night signal, not a lighthouse event, and the story now says so.
